section.title: Woes to the Scribes and Pharisees
section.sectionRationale: Jesus' last public words are a sustained exposure of the religious leaders' hypocrisy. He warns the crowds not to imitate them, pronounces seven woes on scribes and Pharisees who major on externals while neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness, and ends with a grieving lament over Jerusalem.
section.thesis: Religion that polishes the outside while the heart is full of greed and pride is condemned by God, who weighs justice, mercy, and faithfulness; yet even in judgment Jesus grieves over the city that would not be gathered, longing to shelter His people.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the warning against the leaders' hypocrisy and pride; the seven woes on the scribes and Pharisees; and the lament over Jerusalem.

units.label: Do not imitate them
units.note: they do not practice what they preach

verses.text: Then Jesus spoke to the crowds and to His disciples:
“The scribes and Pharisees sit in Moses’ seat.
So practice and observe everything they tell you. But do not do what they do, for they do not practice what they preach.
They tie up heavy, burdensome loads and lay them on men’s shoulders, but they themselves are not willing to lift a finger to move them.
All their deeds are done for men to see. They broaden their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels.
They love the places of honor at banquets, the chief seats in the synagogues,
the greetings in the marketplaces, and the title of ‘Rabbi’ by which they are addressed.
But you are not to be called ‘Rabbi,’ for you have one Teacher, and you are all brothers.
And do not call anyone on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven.
Nor are you to be called instructors, for you have one Instructor, the Christ.
The greatest among you shall be your servant.
For whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

units.label: The seven woes
units.note: outside clean, inside full of greed

verses.text: Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you {{hypokrites|hypocrites}}! You shut the kingdom of heaven in men’s faces. You yourselves do not enter, nor will you let in those who wish to enter.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You traverse land and sea to win a single convert, and when he becomes one, you make him twice as much a son of hell as you are.
Woe to you, blind guides! You say, ‘If anyone swears by the temple, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gold of the temple, he is bound by his oath.’
You blind fools! Which is greater: the gold, or the temple that makes it sacred?
And you say, ‘If anyone swears by the altar, it means nothing; but if anyone swears by the gift on it, he is bound by his oath.’
You blind men! Which is greater: the gift, or the altar that makes it sacred?
So then, he who swears by the altar swears by it and by everything on it.
And he who swears by the temple swears by it and by the One who dwells in it.
And he who swears by heaven swears by God’s throne and by the One who sits on it.

Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You pay tithes of mint, dill, and cumin. But you have disregarded the weightier matters of the law: justice, mercy, and faithfulness. You should have practiced the latter, without neglecting the former.
You blind guides! You strain out a gnat but swallow a camel.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You clean the outside of the cup and dish, but inside they are full of greed and self-indulgence.
Blind Pharisee! First clean the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may become clean as well.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You are like whitewashed tombs, which look beautiful on the outside but on the inside are full of dead men’s bones and every kind of impurity.
In the same way, on the outside you appear to be righteous, but on the inside you are full of hypocrisy and wickedness.
Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites! You build tombs for the prophets and decorate the monuments of the righteous.
And you say, ‘If we had lived in the days of our fathers, we would not have been partners with them in shedding the blood of the prophets.’
So you testify against yourselves that you are the sons of those who murdered the prophets.
Fill up, then, the measure of the sin of your fathers.
You snakes! You brood of vipers! How will you escape the sentence of {{gehenna|hell}}?
Because of this, I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers. Some of them you will kill and crucify, and others you will flog in your synagogues and persecute from town to town.
And so upon you will come all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah son of Berechiah, whom you murdered between the temple and the altar.
Truly I tell you, all these things will come upon this generation.

units.label: Lament over Jerusalem
units.note: how often I have longed to gather you

verses.text: O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her, how often I have longed to {{episynago|gather}} your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!
Look, your house is left to you desolate.
For I tell you that you will not see Me again until you say, ‘Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.’”

hypokrites.gloss: An actor behind a mask, a pretender. The refrain of the woes: the scribes and Pharisees perform righteousness for an audience while their hearts are full of greed and pride, a gap between the outward show and the inner reality that God sees and judges.

gehenna.gloss: Hell, named after the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a place of burning and refuse and, in Israel's past, child sacrifice. Jesus uses it for the final judgment; He asks how those who make converts twice the sons of hell will themselves escape its sentence.

episynago.gloss: To gather together, as a hen gathers her chicks. It expresses Jesus' tender, maternal longing to shelter Jerusalem's children under His wings; the tragedy is not that He was unwilling but that they were.

basic.context: In His final public address, Jesus warns the crowds and disciples about the scribes and Pharisees: they teach God's law but do not live it, loading burdens on others while seeking honor for themselves. He forbids His followers to crave titles and to lord it over others. Then He pronounces seven woes, exposing leaders who shut the kingdom, chase converts, split hairs over oaths, tithe herbs while ignoring justice and mercy, and look clean outside but are corrupt within. He ends grieving over Jerusalem, longing to gather her, yet warning her house is left desolate.
basic.hermeneutics: These woes are not a blanket attack on a people but a prophetic indictment of a particular hypocrisy that can infect any religion, including ours. Notice the recurring contrast of outside and inside, and the weightier matters, justice, mercy, faithfulness, against ceremonial trivia. The closing lament shows the heart behind the severity: judgment grieves the Judge.
basic.originalLanguages: The refrain names the leaders hypokritai, masked actors. Jesus warns of gehenna, hell, the fire of final judgment. And He laments that He longed to episynago, to gather Jerusalem's children like a hen her chicks, but they were unwilling.
basic.typology: Jesus stands in the line of the prophets who denounced hollow worship, but as more than a prophet, sending His own messengers. The hen gathering her chicks echoes God sheltering Israel under His wings.
basic.christ: Jesus is the one Teacher and Instructor, the Christ, the true and humble servant-leader against the proud. He is the sender of prophets, the judge who pronounces the woes, and the grieving Savior who longs to gather His people under His wings.
basic.god: God sees past every performance to the heart and weighs justice, mercy, and faithfulness above outward show. He is patient and pleading, longing to gather, yet just; persistent rejection leaves a house desolate.
basic.crossReferences: Isaiah 29 and Micah 6 weigh true worship against externals. Luke 11 gives parallel woes. Psalm 91 pictures refuge under God's wings. Psalm 118 supplies the closing blessed is He who comes.
basic.oneStory: Jesus' last public words expose a religion of appearances and defend the weightier matters of the heart, warning that God is not mocked by performance. Yet the severity ends in tears: the Judge longs to gather the very city that kills the prophets. The passion is near, and the One who weeps over Jerusalem will soon be crucified by her leaders, gathering His scattered people to Himself through the cross.

context.literary:
Matthew 23 is the last of Jesus' public speeches, and it stands as the dark counterpart of the Sermon on the Mount. The Sermon opened with a run of blessings, 'Blessed are the poor in spirit,' Matthew 5:3 to 11, and this speech is built on a run of woes. The same Gospel that began with the beatitudes of the kingdom ends Jesus' public teaching with the woes of those who shut it. The structure is four parts: an address to the crowds and disciples about how to relate to the leaders, verses 1 to 12; the woes pronounced on the leaders, verses 13 to 36; the lament over Jerusalem, verses 37 to 39; and, in the next chapter, the prediction of the temple's fall.

The woes themselves are arranged with care. In the Greek text the BSB follows, there are seven, in verses 13, 15, 16, 23, 25, 27 and 29, the one in verse 16 being addressed to 'blind guides' rather than to 'hypocrites.' Seven is the number of completeness. Most open with the same formula, 'Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, you hypocrites,' with the repetition working like the beat of a funeral drum. The first two concern the leaders' effect on others, shutting the kingdom and corrupting converts. The middle three concern what they do with the Law, oaths, tithes and purity. The last two concern the inner life and the history of blood: whitewashed tombs and the tombs of the prophets.

The speech turns on a set of contrasts. Outside and inside recur in verses 25 to 28. Greater and lesser run through the oath sayings, 17 to 22, and the tithing saying, 23. Saying and doing frame the whole, verses 3 and 23 to 24. The reversal of status is announced at the start in verses 11 and 12, and the woes themselves enact it. It is a speech about what is truly weighty, and the images of a gnat and a camel, of the cup, and of a tomb all turn on the difference between appearance and reality.

The lament that ends the speech is poetry of a different register. The doubled 'Jerusalem, Jerusalem' recalls the doubled names with which God calls in Scripture, 'Abraham, Abraham' and 'Moses, Moses,' and the passage's last word is not a woe but a promise, verse 39. The words of Psalm 118:26 that opened the entry in 21:9 now close the public ministry, and the whole temple section of Matthew is thus bracketed by the same line from the same psalm.
context.historical:
The scribes were the professional students and copyists of the Law, and many of them belonged to the Pharisaic movement, which sought to extend the holiness of the temple into everyday life. The Pharisees were not a priestly elite but a lay movement with wide popular respect. This is part of why the speech is so shocking: the people criticized are the most devout and best regarded teachers in the land. Jesus' charge is not that they were irreligious but that their religion had become a stage.

The 'seat of Moses' in verse 2 is more than an idiom. Stone seats designated for the teacher have been found in ancient synagogues, including one from Chorazin in Galilee, one of the towns Jesus had condemned earlier, Matthew 11:21. The saying acknowledges that those who sit in it have a legitimate role as teachers of the Law.

Phylacteries are small leather boxes containing passages of Scripture, bound to the forehead and arm in obedience to Exodus 13:9 and Deuteronomy 11:18, and tassels were required on the corners of the cloak by Numbers 15:38-39 and Deuteronomy 22:12. Both were meant to remind the wearer of God's commandments. The accusation is that they have made the reminders larger so as to be seen. Likewise the chief seats of the synagogue and the places of honor at banquets were marks of status in a society where honor was the great currency.

Many of the examples come from the practical life of the Law. Tithing of garden herbs went beyond the plain command of Deuteronomy 14:22 to the careful counting of the smallest produce, and Jesus does not forbid it but says the weightier matters should not be left undone. Straining a gnat out of wine is usually understood as a practice of avoiding ritual impurity, since the insect was unclean, while the camel was also an unclean animal, Leviticus 11:4. The picture is of fussy care over a small impurity while swallowing a large one.

Whitewashing graves was a custom of marking them before Passover so that pilgrims would not touch a grave unknowingly and become unclean for seven days, Numbers 19:16. The whitewash is a warning that something unclean lies beneath, but Jesus turns it into a picture of beautiful hypocrisy. The tombs of the prophets were visited and decorated, and the leaders' protestations about their ancestors have a plausible historical setting in a time when honoring the martyrs was a form of piety. The destruction of the temple in AD 70, about forty years later, gives the closing lament a terrible weight.
context.canonical:
The woe is a prophetic form. Isaiah 5:8-23 contains a run of woes against those who join house to house, who call evil good and good evil, and who are wise in their own eyes. The prophets used it for the grief of anticipated judgment, and the Hebrew word and its Greek rendering carry both anger and sorrow. Jesus stands in this line, and the speech has many echoes of earlier prophets: Isaiah 29:13 on lip honor with a far heart, which Jesus has already applied in Matthew 15:7-9; Micah 6:8 on justice, mercy and walking humbly; Hosea 6:6, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice,' quoted by Jesus in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7; and Ezekiel 34 on the shepherds who feed themselves.

The fault of burdening others with loads echoes Malachi 2:7-9, where the priests who should have preserved knowledge instead caused many to stumble. The seven woes of Matthew 23 are matched in Luke 11:37-52, a smaller set of woes spoken at a Pharisee's table. In Matthew they are public and final. The idea of 'filling up the measure' recalls Genesis 15:16, where the iniquity of the Amorites was 'not yet complete,' and Paul will say in 1 Thessalonians 2:16 that people continue to heap up their sins to full capacity.

The killing of the prophets is a long Old Testament record, Nehemiah 9:26, 2 Chronicles 36:15-16, Jeremiah 26:20-23, and Stephen will repeat the charge in Acts 7:51-52. The reference to Abel and Zechariah brackets the whole record, from the first murder in Genesis 4:10 to the murder of a priest's son in the courtyard in 2 Chronicles 24:20-22.

The lament depends on the Old Testament's image of God sheltering under wings, Deuteronomy 32:11, Ruth 2:12, Psalms 17:8, 36:7, 57:1 and 91:4, and on God's departure from the temple in Ezekiel 11:22-23, where the glory leaves the city and stands over the mountain to the east. 'Your house is left to you desolate' recalls Jeremiah 22:5 and Jeremiah 12:7, where the LORD forsakes His house. The closing 'Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord' is Psalm 118:26 again, and it points forward to the coming of Christ in glory, Matthew 24:30 and 24:31.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Matthew means his readers to see the leaders' failure as a warning with two edges. The first edge cuts against those who held positions of teaching, whose authority Jesus acknowledges and whose conduct He condemns. The second cuts against the church, which has its own seats of honor and its own titles. The first section is addressed 'to the crowds and to His disciples,' and the instruction to call no one rabbi or father or instructor is directed to the community of followers. In the structure of the Gospel, the woes are what the Sermon's blessing looks like when it is refused.

Matthew also wants his readers to take the speech's warnings seriously without turning them into contempt. The hardest language is followed at once by tears. The intention is not to give believers a licence to despise another group but to expose a danger that attaches to every religious establishment, including the one Matthew's church was becoming. The honorific titles, the love of recognition, and the neglect of justice and mercy were as available in the church as in the synagogue.

The author's last point is that the way to avoid the woes is the way of the servant. The first section ends with the great reversal of verses 11 and 12, and the book will end with Jesus Himself taking the path of humiliation and being exalted.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The speech describes a particular group at a particular moment, in the voice of the one who can read hearts. It is not a charter for believers to pronounce woes on their opponents. Jesus is the Judge, and the church is told in the same Gospel not to judge others, Matthew 7:1, and to remove its own beam first, Matthew 7:3-5. The history of the church shows how disastrous it is when this chapter is used as a weapon against Jewish people. Matthew's Jesus speaks as a Jew to Jews about Jewish leaders, and the lament is the grief of a Jerusalem native.

What is prescribed is the self-examination that follows. The instruction in verses 8 to 12 is plain: do not seek titles, call no one father in the sense of ultimate authority, find your greatness in service. It is not a ban on every title or on a child calling a parent father, since Paul speaks of himself as a father to his converts, but a warning about the heart that craves honor. Verse 3 is also instruction: honor what is taught from the Law, and do not imitate the failures of the teachers. And verse 23 gives a way to sort priorities, since the lesser matters of ritual and giving are not abolished, but the weightier matters must come first.

debates.question: Why does Jesus tell the people to obey the Pharisees in verse 3?

views.label: Obey what they teach from Moses' seat
views.case: The sentence says to practice and observe everything they tell you, because they sit in Moses' seat. On this reading Jesus honors the office of teaching the Law while condemning the conduct. The point is that the people should not use the teachers' failure as an excuse for disobedience, and the contrast is between their words and their deeds.

views.label: Ironic or limited: obey only what accords with Moses
views.case: Jesus elsewhere sharply rejects the traditions of the elders when they nullify the Law, Matthew 15:3-9, and the woes show that the Pharisees' teaching on oaths and tithes was flawed. So 'everything' must be understood as everything that truly conveys Moses, with the weight placed on the phrase 'sit in Moses' seat.'

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that Moses' Law stands and that the leaders' teaching is to be measured by it. Jesus is not telling the crowds to follow every rule of the Pharisees but to hear the Law when it is read, and to refuse the example of those who do not live it.

debates.question: Who is Zechariah son of Berechiah?

views.label: Zechariah son of Jehoiada, killed in the courtyard
views.case: 2 Chronicles 24:20-22 tells how the Spirit came on Zechariah son of Jehoiada the priest, and the people stoned him in the courtyard of the temple. Chronicles stands at the end of the Hebrew Scriptures, so the range from Abel in Genesis to Zechariah in Chronicles spans the whole Bible. Luke 11:51 has the name Zechariah without the patronymic. On this view 'son of Berechiah' is a transmission difficulty or a family name that Matthew's source supplied.

views.label: The prophet Zechariah son of Berechiah
views.case: The prophet of the book of Zechariah is the son of Berechiah, Zechariah 1:1. Some have suggested that tradition gave him a martyr's death in the temple, though the Old Testament does not record it.

views.label: A conflation of two men named Zechariah
views.case: Others hold that Matthew or his source has merged the priest of Chronicles with the prophet of the same name, so that the father's name has slipped. Josephus tells of a Zechariah son of Baruch killed in the temple during the war of AD 66 to 70, but that is later than this speech and so cannot be what Jesus meant.

debates.bearing: The Gospel text does not resolve the problem, and we should hold the answer loosely. The most natural fit with 'between the temple and the altar' and 'whom you murdered' is the murder in the temple court in Chronicles. What matters for the sense is that the whole record of innocent blood, from first to last, falls on a generation that has the opportunity to repent.

debates.question: What does verse 39 promise Jerusalem?

views.label: A future repentance and welcome
views.case: The sentence says they will not see Him again until they say 'Blessed is He who comes.' Paul speaks of a hardening in part until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and says that all Israel will be saved, Romans 11:25-26. On this view the verse closes the lament with a hope that Jerusalem will one day welcome Him.

views.label: A forced acknowledgment at the judgment
views.case: The acclamation will come at His return when every knee bows, Philippians 2:10-11, and will be the confession of the defeated as well as the joy of the saved. The verse then expresses the certainty of vindication, without promising conversion.

views.label: Already beginning in the crowd's Hosanna
views.case: Some see the cry already uttered at the entry, 21:9, as the fulfilment, with 23:39 pointing to those who will welcome Him as His disciples preach after the resurrection.

debates.bearing: The verse leaves the door open. Whatever the final shape, the word 'until' means that rejection is not the last word. The same Lord who pronounces woe also promises that there will be a day when His coming is greeted with blessing.

study.originalLanguages:
The word translated 'hypocrites' is hypokrites, and in Greek it was the word for an actor, from a verb that means to answer from beneath, then to play a part on stage. The Greek stage actors wore masks, so the term carries the sense of someone speaking in a borrowed voice and face. The word in Matthew is not simply for a person who falls short of his ideals, since everyone does, but for a person who lives for the audience. Jesus has used it before: of those who give and pray to be seen, Matthew 6:2 and 5, and of the critic with a beam in his own eye, Matthew 7:5.

The refrain 'Woe' is ouai, an exclamation both of grief and of warning, which the Greek Old Testament uses for the prophetic woes of Isaiah 5. It is not the same as a curse. The ancient hearer would feel the sorrow in it as well as the threat, which is why the lament can follow without contradiction. The seven woes announce what is coming and grieve over it.

In verse 10 the 'instructors' are kathegetai, guides or leaders, a term for one who goes ahead and shows the way. The one true guide is the Christ. The verse is the culmination of the three prohibitions, 'Rabbi,' 'father,' 'instructor,' each of which names a different kind of dependence, and the statement that 'you are all brothers' in verse 8 uses the plain word adelphoi for those of a single family.

In verse 15 the convert is a prosélytos, a proselyte, one who has come over to Judaism. The phrase 'son of hell' is a Semitic idiom meaning someone destined for or belonging to Gehenna, as in the phrase 'son of peace.' The word Gehenna is the Greek form of the Hebrew for the Valley of Hinnom, south of Jerusalem, where children had been burned in the fire in Topheth, Jeremiah 7:31-32. Jeremiah promised that it would be called the Valley of Slaughter. It became a figure for the place of final judgment, and Jesus uses it in Matthew 5:22 and 10:28 as well. Its use in verse 33, 'the sentence of Gehenna,' is the language of a court.

The saying about the gnat and the camel in verse 24 depends on a contrast of scale. The Greek has the guides 'straining out' the gnat, diylizo, which is a word for filtering liquid, and 'swallowing' the camel. The two animals are both unclean, and the picture is of a comic inversion of priorities. Verse 23 names the weightier matters of the Law as krisis, justice, eleos, mercy, and pistis, faithfulness. The middle word, eleos, is the one Jesus has quoted from Hosea 6:6 twice, and it is the word that translates the covenant love of the Old Testament. Notice also that he says these were to be done 'without neglecting the former,' so the tithing is not condemned.

The cleaning of the cup in verses 25 and 26 and the whitewashed tombs in verses 27 and 28 give us the contrast of 'outside' and 'inside.' The inside of the cup is full of harpage, plunder or robbery, and akrasia, lack of self-control, the BSB's 'greed and self-indulgence.' The tombs are 'whitewashed,' a word that appears in the Greek of Acts 23:3 when Paul calls the high priest a whitewashed wall. The woes name inner conditions, 'hypocrisy and wickedness' in verse 28, with the word anomia, lawlessness, a word Matthew uses for the opposite of obedience, Matthew 7:23 and 24:12. The irony is that those most zealous for the Law are called lawless within.

In verse 32, 'Fill up the measure' is an imperative that sounds like permission but is a declaration of what the leaders are already doing. The verb for 'fill up' is pleroo, the same verb that Matthew uses for the fulfilment of Scripture, and the echo is likely intended, since the history of the killing of prophets will be completed. In verse 34 Jesus says 'I am sending,' with a verb of commissioning, apostello, so that He takes to Himself the sending of prophets, wise men and teachers. Luke attributes a similar saying to the wisdom of God, Luke 11:49.

The lament uses the verb episynago, 'to gather together,' and the same verb appears for the gathering of the elect by the angels in Matthew 24:31. The hen is ornis and the chicks nossia, and the image is of a mother bird covering her brood under her wings, an image that the Psalms apply to God's protection. The tragic verb is thelo, 'to will': 'I willed to gather... and you were not willing,' which in the Greek is the same verb twice, in the first person and then in the second. The divine will meets the human will, and the human will prevails to the point of the house being left desolate. Note the shift in verse 38 from 'My house' in Matthew 21:13 to 'your house.'

typology.type: The prophets who are killed and the sending of more
typology.fulfillment: From Abel to Zechariah the Old Testament records the blood of the righteous, Genesis 4:10 and 2 Chronicles 24:20-22. Jesus places Himself at the end of this line, as the one who sends prophets and wise men and teachers, and who will be killed as they were. The correspondence is that rejection of God's messengers is a repeated pattern, and the escalation is that Jesus is not the last prophet but the Lord who commissions them. Acts 7:51-52 and 1 Thessalonians 2:15 show the pattern continuing into the church's own experience. The type is exceeded in that the blood shed in Jerusalem is eventually answered by blood that speaks better than Abel's, Hebrews 12:24.

typology.type: The hen and her chicks, the wings of God
typology.fulfillment: Israel's songs picture God sheltering His people under His wings, Psalm 91:4, Psalm 36:7, Ruth 2:12, and the eagle of Deuteronomy 32:11 spreads its wings over its young. Jesus takes this picture of God's care and says it is His own longing for Jerusalem. The correspondence is not that He is merely like God but that He speaks the very longing of God. The escalation is that the wings are the cross, where He gathers 'His elect' and the scattered children of God, Matthew 24:31 and John 11:52. The type falls short in that a hen protects by sitting while the storm passes, whereas Jesus gathers by bearing the storm Himself.

typology.type: The glory leaving the temple, the house left desolate
typology.fulfillment: In Ezekiel 11:22-23 the glory of the LORD rose from the city and stood over the mountain east of it, and Jeremiah 12:7 and 22:5 speak of the LORD forsaking His house. The words 'your house is left to you desolate' in verse 38 continue this story. Jesus leaves the temple at the start of chapter 24 and sits on the Mount of Olives, the mountain east of the city, Matthew 24:1-3. The correspondence is striking. The escalation is that the glory has now stood in the temple in the flesh and has been rejected. The type is resolved in the new creation, where the dwelling place of God is with man, Revelation 21:3.

typology.type: The shepherds who feed themselves, and the shepherd who gathers
typology.fulfillment: Ezekiel 34:2-4 denounces shepherds who feed themselves, do not strengthen the weak or search for the lost, and rule with violence. The leaders of Matthew 23 who burden others and love honor are those shepherds. Ezekiel's remedy is that God Himself will search for His sheep, and Isaiah 40:11 says He gathers the lambs in His arms. Jesus fulfills this in being the Shepherd who seeks the lost, Matthew 18:12-14, and who lays down His life for the sheep, John 10:11. The type is exceeded in that God's own gathering is accomplished in a human Shepherd who is also the Lamb.

study.christ:
This chapter reveals Christ as Teacher, Judge and Shepherd, and as the one who is greater than the temple. The opening instruction, 'you have one Teacher... one Instructor, the Christ,' places Him alone at the head of the community. It echoes the Gospel's earlier commission at the transfiguration, 'listen to Him,' Matthew 17:5. The disciples are brothers under one Teacher, and the title that the leaders crave belongs finally to Him.

The speech also shows Christ as the one who humbles Himself. 'Whoever humbles himself will be exalted' is a statement of the principle of His own life. Paul puts it in the hymn of Philippians 2:5-8: though in the form of God, He emptied Himself, took the form of a servant, and became obedient to death on a cross, and therefore God exalted Him. What He asks of the disciples, that the greatest be the servant, He has done first, and what He tells them in Matthew 20:28, that the Son of Man came to serve and to give His life as a ransom for many, is the key to the speech. The woes expose the opposite way, the way that seeks honor, and the Messiah shows the way that does not.

He is the Judge. The one who says 'woe' is the one who will say 'I never knew you' at the last, Matthew 7:23, and who will sit on the throne of His glory, Matthew 25:31. Yet the Judge is the one who weeps. The lament shows a divine heart, since the one who longs to gather is speaking the longing of God for His people. Luke records that Jesus wept as He approached the city, Luke 19:41. The tears do not soften the verdict, but they show what it costs.

He is the sender of prophets and the one who will be killed like them. 'I am sending you prophets and wise men and teachers' is the speech of one who stands above the prophets. Hebrews makes the contrast that God spoke through prophets and in these last days through a Son, Hebrews 1:1-2. The one who says 'some of them you will kill and crucify' is also naming His own coming death, since crucifixion is the form of execution awaiting Him.

He is the gathering Savior. 'How often I have longed to gather your children' is not only an expression of feeling but a statement of mission. He gathers by the cross and resurrection and sends His angels to gather the elect from the four winds, Matthew 24:31. The blessing that is promised in verse 39 is not a mere hope but the substance of the Christian proclamation: Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord.

We should be careful not to read every detail as a type. The cups and tombs are illustrations from daily life, not coded references. The Christological weight lies in what Jesus says about Himself: the one Teacher, the servant who is exalted, the sender of prophets, the Judge who grieves, and the Shepherd who gathers.
study.god:
The chapter shows that God cares about the inside of a person more than the outside. The cup must be clean within, the tomb must hold no corruption, and the heart must be turned to Him. This is the consistent teaching of the Law and the Prophets, from Samuel's word that the LORD looks at the heart, 1 Samuel 16:7, to Isaiah's complaint that people honor Him with their lips while their hearts are far away, Isaiah 29:13. A God who sees the heart cannot be impressed by display, and no amount of religious activity can stand in for what He asks.

The chapter also shows what God weighs. Justice, mercy and faithfulness are the weightier matters, and they are not new teaching. They are what Micah 6:8 says the LORD requires, and what the prophets say He wants rather than sacrifice. God does not despise the lesser matters, the tithe of herbs, but He holds them in order. The ordering of duties is a window into His character: He is a God of justice who defends the widow and the orphan, and a God of mercy who forgives.

God is just. The woes are real, and the judgment that falls on a generation is the consequence of a long record. The blood of the righteous is not forgotten, and the God who heard Abel's blood cry from the ground, Genesis 4:10, takes account of every innocent death. His patience has a limit, not because He is capricious but because He is righteous. The statement that the measure is being filled shows a God who waits and then acts, as He did with the Amorites in Genesis 15:16.

God is also tender. The metaphor of the mother bird is among the gentlest in Scripture, and it is applied to the same God who pronounces woe. The sentence 'how often I have longed' reveals persistent, unforced desire, and the final line, 'you were unwilling,' respects the creature's will. God does not override it. The tension between divine longing and human refusal is real in this text and should not be resolved by explaining away either side. The holy God who judges and the compassionate God who longs are the same God, and the lament is where the two meet.

For worship, the passage asks us to examine our own hearts before God before we turn to those of others. It calls us to honor Him with more than words, to pursue justice and mercy, and to receive the invitation in verse 37, to be gathered. It also asks us to hold in tension a holy fear of the God who sees what is hidden and a childlike trust in the God who shelters under His wings.

crossReferences.note: The people draw near with their mouths and honor God with their lips, but their hearts are far from Him, and their worship is a set of rules taught by men. Jesus applies this to the Pharisees in Matthew 15:7-9, and the seven woes can be read as an extended commentary on the verse.

What does the LORD require? To act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God. The weightier matters of Matthew 23:23 are this verse in New Testament dress, and the contrast with the obsession over small things is exactly Micah's contrast with burnt offerings.

I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings. Jesus has quoted this twice already, in Matthew 9:13 and 12:7, against the same group. It is the principle that governs the choice between the gnat and the camel.

The tassels were meant to help Israel remember all the LORD's commandments and not to follow their own hearts and eyes. Jesus' complaint in Matthew 23:5 is that the leaders lengthen the tassels as a show. A sign meant to remind the wearer has become a sign meant to impress the watcher.

The voice of Abel's blood cries out from the ground. Jesus begins His list of murdered righteous people with Abel, and the verse explains why the blood is said to 'come upon' a generation: God hears it and calls to account.

Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the courtyard of the house of the LORD, and as he died he asked that the LORD see it and call the king to account. The Chronicles story fits the place named in Matthew 23:35 and ends the Hebrew Bible's record of martyrs.

The Valley of Hinnom, where children were burned in Topheth, would be renamed the Valley of Slaughter. Gehenna, the word Jesus uses for final judgment in Matthew 23:33, is the Greek form of this place name, and Jeremiah's oracle explains why it became an image of judgment.

Woe to the shepherds who feed themselves, who do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick or search for the lost. The charge matches the picture of leaders who tie up heavy loads and will not lift a finger to move them, and the remedy in the chapter is that God will shepherd His sheep Himself.

He will cover you with His feathers, and under His wings you will find refuge. The psalm gives the image behind the hen and her chicks, and Jesus speaks the divine care in the first person: how often I have longed to gather your children.

If the house does not hear these words, the LORD swears by Himself that it will become a pile of rubble. The sentence 'your house is left to you desolate' in verse 38 continues the prophetic warning that God would abandon a house that He once filled with His glory.

A related set of woes spoken at a Pharisee's table, with the same charges about tithes, burdens, and the tombs of the prophets, and the saying about the wisdom of God sending prophets and apostles. The comparison shows how Matthew has gathered and arranged Jesus' teaching for his last public speech.

The mind of Christ is the opposite of the leaders' mind. He did not grasp at status but emptied Himself, took the form of a servant and was obedient to death on a cross. The saying that whoever humbles himself will be exalted is the law of His own life.

study.oneStory:
At the beginning, God made human beings to be His image in the world and to know Him, and the first sin was a refusal to receive what God said as good. Ever since, religion has been a place where that refusal hides. The story of Scripture includes the way that people use even the Law, the temple and the sacrifices to keep God at a distance while looking close. The prophets named this again and again, and Matthew 23 is where the long record of prophetic complaint reaches its sharpest form.

The speech also carries the history of the prophets forward. From Abel to Zechariah the blood of the righteous has been shed, and God has sent His servants again and again, and now sends the last of them. This is the story that the parable of the tenants told in the previous chapters, and it leads straight to the cross. Jesus names His own coming death within the pattern and calls it the filling up of a measure.

Yet the passage does not end in condemnation. The lament shows the same God who walked in the garden and who carried Israel on eagles' wings still reaching out. The word 'until' in the last verse keeps the future open, and the New Testament shows that the gathering did happen: the same Jerusalem heard the preaching of the apostles, and thousands responded. Paul says that a hardening has come on part of Israel until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in, and that all Israel will be saved, Romans 11:25-26.

The woes also prepare for the church's own calling. The new community is to be marked by service rather than titles, by justice, mercy and faithfulness, and by clean hearts and not merely clean cups. This is the community of one Teacher, one Father and one Instructor, in which there is neither Jew nor Greek, Galatians 3:28, and one body and one Spirit, Ephesians 4:4-6.

The ending of the Bible answers the lament. The glory that left the city in Ezekiel returns, and the dwelling place of God is with man, Revelation 21:3. The city that killed the prophets is replaced by a city where nothing unclean enters and the people are gathered from every nation, Revelation 21:27 and 7:9. The Lord who was hailed with Hosanna and wept at the gate welcomes His people home, and the longing 'how often I have longed to gather' is finally satisfied.

quiz.q: What was the central charge in Jesus' woes against the scribes and Pharisees?

options.text: Hypocrisy: they polished the outside while their hearts were full of greed and pride.
options.note: The repeated word hypocrites and the outside-inside contrast define the woes.

options.text: They taught the law of Moses to the people.
options.note: Jesus said to observe what they teach from Moses' seat; the fault was their hypocritical lives, not teaching the law.

options.text: They were too strict in keeping God's commandments.
options.note: They were scrupulous about trivia but neglected justice and mercy; the problem was misplaced emphasis, not excess obedience.
They were intensely religious; the problem was hypocrisy, not irreligion.

quiz.q: What are the weightier matters of the law the leaders neglected?

options.note: Verse 23 names these against the tithing of mint, dill, and cumin.

options.text: Careful tithing of even the smallest herbs.
options.note: Jesus said not to neglect the tithing, but the weightier matters are justice, mercy, and faithfulness, which this reverses.
Ritual precision is the lesser matter here; the weightier ones concern the heart and neighbor.

options.text: Wearing broad phylacteries and long tassels.
options.note: Those were the showy externals Jesus condemned, not the weightier matters.

quiz.q: How does Jesus want greatness expressed among His followers?

options.text: In humble service, since the one who humbles himself will be exalted.
options.note: Verses 11-12 set service and humility against the leaders' craving for honor.

options.text: In earning respected titles like Rabbi and teacher.
options.note: The opposite; Jesus warns against craving such titles, pointing to one Teacher.

options.text: In taking the chief seats and public greetings.
options.note: These are exactly the honors Jesus rebukes the leaders for loving.

options.text: In quietly avoiding all responsibility for others.
options.note: Greatness is active service of others, not withdrawal from them.

quiz.q: What does Jesus' lament over Jerusalem reveal?

options.text: A grieving love that longed to gather the city, even as it faced judgment for rejecting Him.
options.note: Verse 37 shows Jesus' tender longing, met by the city's unwillingness.

options.text: That Jesus had given up all concern for Jerusalem.
options.note: The lament shows deep concern and longing, not indifference; judgment grieves Him.

options.text: That the judgment on Jerusalem was unjust.
options.note: The judgment is just; the lament reveals sorrow, not injustice.

options.text: That Jerusalem had always welcomed God's messengers.
options.note: Jesus says the city kills the prophets and was unwilling to be gathered.

questions: Jesus condemned doing deeds to be seen by others. Where do you catch yourself performing your faith for an audience rather than living it before God?
The leaders tithed herbs but neglected justice and mercy. What small religious details might you be using to distract from weightier matters God is asking of you?
Jesus contrasts the clean outside with the corrupt inside. If God cleaned the inside of your cup first, what would He start with?
Greatness is service, and the humble will be exalted. Where is pride shaping your desire for recognition, and what would humble service look like instead?
Jesus wept over the city that rejected Him, longing to gather it. How does the grieving heart of Christ move you toward those who resist Him, including yourself in your resistance?

translationNotes.note: The BSB numbering goes from verse 13 to verse 15; verse 14, about devouring widows' houses and making long prayers, is not in the earliest manuscripts and appears as a footnote drawn from Mark 12:40 and Luke 20:47.

From Abel to Zechariah spans the martyred righteous across the Hebrew Scriptures, from Genesis to Chronicles, the last book in the Hebrew ordering, so the phrase means all the righteous blood ever shed.
Some manuscripts read simply your house is left to you; the word desolate makes explicit the coming abandonment and destruction of the temple, foretold in the next chapter.
